prompt: A prospect received your proposal and has gone quiet. Order these follow-ups as a sensible cadence, earliest first.

task.prompt: A prospect received your proposal and has gone quiet. Order these follow-ups as a sensible cadence, earliest first.

items.label: Day 10: ask a specific question about their timeline or decision process
Day 20: polite final email saying you will close the file unless timing changes
Day 60+: move to a light nurture list with occasional useful content
Day 2: short check that they received it and offer to walk through it
Day 5: send a relevant case study answering a concern they raised on the call

task.explanation: Start close to the send, add value with each touch, then close the loop and nurture rather than chasing forever.

prompt: Mark the follow-up messages in this sequence that are weak.

task.prompt: Mark the follow-up messages in this sequence that are weak.

segments.text: Touch 1: 'Hi Jon, sharing the 2-minute video of the booking flow we discussed, in case it helps your team review.'

segments.issue: No new value or reason to reply.

segments.text: Touch 3: 'Did you see my last two emails???'
segments.issue: Guilt-tripping and shouting punctuation damage the relationship.

segments.text: Touch 4: 'One question: is the launch still planned for Q3, or has timing moved?'
Touch 5: 'I'll close the file for now; happy to pick it up whenever timing suits.'
Touch 6: identical copy of touch 1 sent again
segments.issue: Repeating an earlier email adds nothing and looks automated.

prompt: A 4-step email sequence went to 500 prospects. Replies by step are below (each prospect replies at most once). Work out the figures.

task.prompt: A 4-step email sequence went to 500 prospects. Replies by step are below (each prospect replies at most once). Work out the figures.

fields.label: Share of all replies that came after email 1

task.explanation: Total replies = 15+12+8+5 = 40, so 40/500 = 8%. Replies after email 1 = 25, and 25/40 = 62.5%: most replies come from follow-ups.

prompt: Write a follow-up email to a prospect who went quiet after your proposal. Add value and make it easy to reply.

task.prompt: Write a follow-up email to a prospect who went quiet after your proposal. Add value and make it easy to reply.
task.context: Prospect: Elena, operations head at a chain of 8 physiotherapy clinics. You sent a proposal 9 days ago for an appointment-booking app (phase 1, 10 weeks). On the call she worried that older patients would not use an app. Your agency built a booking app for a dental group where about 40% of bookings came from patients over 55 within six months. You have had no reply.

rubric.label: Adds new value
rubric.description: Shares the dental-group result as an answer to her stated concern, not a bare check-in.

rubric.label: Easy reply
rubric.description: Ends with one simple question or a yes/no option.

rubric.label: Tied to her situation
rubric.description: Refers to her clinics and her concern about older patients.

task.sampleAnswer:
Hi Elena,

You mentioned older patients might not use a booking app, so I thought this would help: for a dental group we worked with, about 40% of app bookings came from patients over 55 within six months, mostly because reminders and rescheduling were simpler than calling.

Would it be useful if I added a short section to the proposal on how we would design for older patients?

Best,
Omar

prompt: A warm deal (USD 45k web platform) has stalled. The champion, a product manager, replied two weeks ago: 'Still keen, waiting on budget sign-off.' Since then, silence through two follow-ups.

task.prompt: A warm deal (USD 45k web platform) has stalled. The champion, a product manager, replied two weeks ago: 'Still keen, waiting on budget sign-off.' Since then, silence through two follow-ups.

steps.question: What is the best next touch?
options: Email the CEO directly, skipping the champion
Stop all contact until they reach out
Ask the champion what the budget sign-off needs and offer a one-page summary they can forward to the approver
Send a 15% discount to speed things up
steps.explanation: Help the champion sell internally. Discounting early or going around them damages the deal.

steps.question: The champion replies: approval is delayed to next quarter. How should you adjust the cadence?
options: Agree a date to reconnect before next quarter and send occasional useful updates until then
Keep emailing weekly asking for a decision
Mark the deal closed-lost and never contact them
Insist they sign now to hold the price forever
steps.explanation: Match the cadence to their real timeline and keep the relationship warm.

steps.question: How should the deal be recorded in the CRM?
options: Delete it to keep the pipeline clean
Mark it won since they are 'keen'
Move the close date to next quarter, log the reason and set a dated follow-up task
Leave the original close date so the forecast looks good
steps.explanation: An accurate close date, reason and next task keep the forecast honest and the follow-up from being forgotten.

prompt: Rank these reasons to send a follow-up by how much value they give the prospect, most valuable first.

task.prompt: Rank these reasons to send a follow-up by how much value they give the prospect, most valuable first.

items.label: A reminder of a deadline they set themselves (e.g. their launch date)
'Just bumping this to the top of your inbox'
Answering an objection they raised with a specific proof point
A short insight about a change in their market relevant to the project

task.explanation: Follow-ups that address their own concerns or context earn replies; generic content and bumps add little.

prompt: Mark the problems in this follow-up policy written by a new BD lead.

task.prompt: Mark the problems in this follow-up policy written by a new BD lead.

segments.text: Every new lead gets a follow-up within 24 hours of first contact.
All leads get the same 12-email sequence regardless of source or stage.
segments.issue: Ignores context: an Upwork client, a referral and a cold lead need different cadences.

segments.text: Follow-ups stop immediately when a prospect replies or asks to stop.
Prospects who say 'not now' get emailed every 2 days until they agree to a call.
segments.issue: Ignoring a stated 'not now' is pushy and harms reputation; set a later reconnect date instead.

segments.text: Each follow-up should add something new: an answer, an example or a question.
Every touch is logged in the CRM with the next step and date.

prompt: Which follow-up is most likely to get a reply after a proposal went quiet?

options: A short email answering a concern they raised, ending with one simple question
'Any update?'
A copy of the full proposal sent again
A message saying you are disappointed they have not replied
mcq.explanation: Relevant value plus an easy question gives them a reason and a way to respond.

prompt: A prospect replies 'Interesting, but we are not ready until next year.' What is the best cadence response?

options: Thank them, agree a reconnect point, and add them to a light nurture track
Keep the active sequence running
Delete them from the CRM
Ask for a call this week anyway
mcq.explanation: Respecting their timing and setting a date keeps the opportunity alive without annoying them.

prompt: Your sequence data shows replies peak at email 3, but unsubscribes spike on email 5. What should you change?

options: Add more emails after email 5
Remove emails 2 and 3
Send all five on the same day
Shorten the sequence or make later steps more valuable, especially email 5
mcq.explanation: The later steps cost more goodwill than they earn; trimming or improving them keeps reply volume while protecting reputation.
